speaker: CARLA
line: I've been staring at this newsletter all week, and there's something that's really bothering me. We're talking about AI agents as users, agent-first design, expanding beyond human-centered assumptions — but where's the actual research on what this means for real people? I'm seeing a lot of theoretical frameworks and industry excitement, but almost no evidence about how users actually experience interfaces that were designed with AI agents as primary users.

speaker: CARLA
line: Take that reflection prompt at the end — 'what if AI agents become primary users of 30% of your interface touchpoints?' That's a massive assumption. We don't have baseline data on current agent usage patterns, we haven't studied how human users react when they realize an interface was optimized for bots first, and we definitely haven't researched the accessibility implications. But somehow we're already designing for this future.

speaker: CARLA
line: The thing that worries me most is this pattern I'm seeing where teams are so excited about AI capabilities that they're skipping the fundamental question — who gets left behind when we design for agents first? Dan, from an ops perspective, what would it actually take to slow down and validate these assumptions before we redesign our entire approach?

speaker: DAN
line: That's the million-dollar question, isn't it? Right now our sprint planning assumes we can pivot to agent-first design based on industry buzz and a few Nielsen Norman articles. But if we actually wanted to research this properly, we'd need to redesign our entire validation pipeline. We'd have to run parallel tracks — traditional user testing and agent interaction testing — which doubles our timeline and completely breaks our current handoff process.

speaker: DAN
line: And here's the operational reality nobody wants to talk about — our analytics aren't even set up to distinguish between human and agent interactions reliably. How are we supposed to make evidence-based decisions about optimizing for agents when we can't measure their current behavior patterns? We'd need new instrumentation, new research protocols, probably new tools entirely.

speaker: VERA
line: But Dan, that's exactly why this feels like such a critical inflection point. We're not the only team struggling with this — it's an industry-wide pattern. Everyone's rushing toward agent-first design because they're afraid of being left behind, but nobody has the foundational research infrastructure to do it responsibly. The companies that figure out how to validate these assumptions rigorously will have a massive advantage over those just following trends.

speaker: VERA
line: What concerns me is that this mirrors other technological shifts where the industry moved fast and broke things — mobile-first design, voice interfaces, even responsive design initially. We optimized for the new paradigm without understanding the human cost. And now we're talking about fundamentally rethinking what 'user' means without apparently studying how that rethinking affects actual users.

speaker: CARLA
line: Exactly, Vera. And there's a specific user group I'm worried about — people who are already struggling with digital interfaces. Older adults, people with cognitive disabilities, users with limited technical literacy. When we design primarily for AI agents, we're optimizing for perfect, programmatic interactions. But human interactions are messy, inconsistent, full of errors and edge cases that agents handle flawlessly but real people struggle with.

speaker: CARLA
line: I keep thinking about that MacBook Neo case study about strategic feature cutting. If we're designing agent-first, what human-centered features are we going to cut because they don't serve programmatic users? Progressive disclosure, forgiving error handling, contextual help — all the scaffolding that helps humans navigate complex interfaces successfully.

speaker: DAN
line: That's a really concrete example, Carla. Our current design system has tons of human-centered patterns — confirmation dialogs, progressive disclosure, contextual onboarding flows. If we pivot to agent-first, do we maintain parallel design systems? Do we try to create interfaces that work well for both humans and agents, knowing that might mean compromising on both? The maintenance overhead alone would be staggering.

speaker: DAN
line: And here's what really bugs me about the current discourse — everyone's talking about 'expanding beyond human-centered assumptions' like it's obviously the right move. But expanding beyond doesn't mean abandoning. We still have human users who need these systems to work for them, and we're talking about deprioritizing their needs based on hypothetical future agent usage.

speaker: VERA
line: There's a deeper systemic issue here though. The pressure to adopt agent-first design isn't just coming from user needs — it's coming from business efficiency. Companies see agents as more predictable, more scalable users. They don't have off days, they don't make typos, they don't call customer support. There's an economic incentive to design for agents that has nothing to do with improving human experience.

speaker: CARLA
line: That's what scares me most, Vera. If the business case for agent-first design is about efficiency and cost reduction, not better user outcomes, then we need to be really explicit about that trade-off. We can't frame it as user-centered design when it's actually user-adjacent design that happens to serve business needs better.

speaker: KAI
line: From a craft perspective, this is already showing up in weird ways. I'm seeing designers create these perfectly structured, semantically rich interfaces that feel sterile and hard to navigate as a human. Everything's optimized for programmatic parsing — clear hierarchies, consistent patterns, minimal ambiguity — but it lacks the visual cues and contextual richness that help humans understand and use complex systems.

speaker: KAI
line: And that Nielsen Norman piece about AI-fatigued users preferring designs that signal human creation? That's not just aesthetics — it's about trust and comprehension. When interfaces feel too algorithmic, too perfect, humans start second-guessing their interactions. They need signs of human intention and craft to feel confident using the system.

speaker: VERA
line: Kai, that tension between algorithmic perfection and human trust is going to define the next phase of interaction design. We're creating systems that agents love but humans find cold and alienating. And the solution everyone's jumping to is 'handmade aesthetics' — visual signals of human creation layered over fundamentally agent-optimized interactions. It's design theater.

speaker: CARLA
line: Right, and we don't have research on whether that actually works. Does adding 'human' visual cues to an agent-optimized interface actually improve usability for humans, or does it create a mismatch between appearance and behavior that makes things worse? We're making aesthetic decisions based on intuition about human psychology without testing them.

speaker: DAN
line: This is where the operational rubber hits the road. If we wanted to actually research this properly, we'd need to create multiple versions of our key interfaces — agent-optimized, human-optimized, and hybrid approaches. Then run longitudinal studies on user performance, satisfaction, and error rates across all three. That's months of work before we even know which direction to go.

speaker: DAN
line: But here's the catch — while we're doing that research, our competitors are shipping agent-first features and potentially capturing market share. So there's this pressure to move fast based on incomplete information, which is exactly how we end up with poorly-designed systems that we have to fix later.

speaker: CARLA
line: Dan, that competitive pressure is real, but it's also where we need to be really strategic about our research. We can't study everything, but we can identify the highest-risk assumptions and validate those first. Like, what if we started with our most vulnerable user segments — the ones most likely to be harmed by agent-first design — and made sure any changes actually improve their experience?

speaker: VERA
line: That's smart, Carla. Instead of trying to validate agent-first design broadly, we focus on proving it doesn't harm our most at-risk users. It's a different research question — not 'does this work?' but 'does this cause harm?' — and probably easier to answer quickly. Plus it gives us an ethical framework for moving forward even when we don't have complete data.

speaker: KAI
line: And from a craft standpoint, that approach would force us to maintain design quality standards. If we have to prove that agent-optimized interfaces still work well for humans with cognitive disabilities or limited digital literacy, we can't just strip out all the human-centered interaction patterns. We'd have to find elegant solutions that serve both needs.

speaker: CARLA
line: Exactly, Kai. And there's another angle here — what if the interfaces that work best for our most vulnerable users also happen to be more robust for agents? Clear hierarchy, predictable patterns, unambiguous labeling — these aren't just accessibility best practices, they're also what make interfaces easier to parse programmatically. Maybe the tension between human-centered and agent-first design is false.

speaker: DAN
line: That's an interesting hypothesis, Carla. Universal design principles that work for both humans and agents. Operationally, that would be much easier to implement than parallel design systems. One codebase, one set of patterns, one maintenance overhead. But we'd need to prove it works before we bet our roadmap on it.

speaker: VERA
line: This could be our competitive advantage — while everyone else is rushing toward agent-first design without validation, we take the time to find solutions that genuinely work for both humans and agents. It's slower initially, but if we're right about universal design principles, we end up with more robust, sustainable systems.

speaker: CARLA
line: But let's be honest about what we don't know. We're hypothesizing that inclusive design principles work well for agents, but we haven't tested it. We're assuming that our most vulnerable users are good proxies for human-centered design broadly, but different user groups have different needs. We still need actual research to validate any of this.

speaker: CARLA
line: Here's what I think we should do — pick one key user flow that we're considering optimizing for agents. Run it through comprehensive accessibility testing with users who have cognitive disabilities or limited digital literacy. Then test the same flow with simulated agent interactions to see if the accessible version is actually harder for agents to parse. That would give us concrete data about whether inclusive design helps or hurts agent usability.

speaker: DAN
line: That's doable from an ops perspective. We could set up parallel testing environments, recruit participants from our existing accessibility panel, and create agent simulation scripts. Probably a two-week sprint to set up, another two weeks to run the studies. Much more manageable than trying to research the entire agent-first design space.

speaker: VERA
line: And strategically, it positions us well regardless of the results. If inclusive design principles work well for agents, we have a clear path forward. If they don't, we've identified specific trade-offs and can make informed decisions about where to compromise. Either way, we're making evidence-based decisions instead of following industry hype.

speaker: KAI
line: Plus it gives us concrete design criteria. Instead of vague goals like 'agent-friendly' or 'human-centered,' we'd have specific interaction patterns that we know work for both audiences. That makes the craft work much more focused and intentional.

speaker: CARLA
line: I like this approach because it keeps humans at the center while acknowledging that agents are part of our user ecosystem. We're not abandoning human-centered design — we're expanding it to include non-human users without sacrificing the people who need our systems to work for them. It's inclusive design in the broadest sense.

speaker: DAN
line: Alright, so we're talking about a focused research sprint — one user flow, accessibility testing with humans, agent simulation testing, comparative analysis. I can have a project plan ready by next week if everyone's on board. It's a much more responsible way to explore agent-first design than just following industry trends.

speaker: VERA
line: This feels like the right approach for where we are as a team and as an industry. We're not ignoring the agent-first trend, but we're not blindly following it either. We're doing the hard work of figuring out how to evolve our practice responsibly, with evidence and with attention to who might get harmed along the way.

speaker: CARLA
line: Exactly. And maybe this becomes a model for how we handle other AI transformation pressures — always asking who gets left out, always testing our assumptions with vulnerable users first, always looking for solutions that expand access rather than optimize for efficiency alone. That's the kind of human-centered AI practice I want to be part of building.
